questions.q: What kind of course is Engineering 509 B?
options: A Brief Foundations mathematics course in Anderson Engineering: an overview and six lectures, about an hour
An optional elective outside the Foundations
questions.explain:
Paragraph 0.1: Paragraph 0.1 gives the format.
A is wrong: A Brief course is a first hour.
C is wrong: It is a Foundations course.
D is wrong: It is a lecture course.

questions.q: What is the backbone of this course?
options: MIT OpenCourseWare 18.05, Introduction to Probability and Statistics, Spring 2014
questions.explain:
Paragraph 0.9: The overview credits Dr Jeremy Orloff and Dr Jonathan Bloom.
A is wrong: That backs Linear Algebra.
C is wrong: That backs Differential Equations.
D is wrong: That backs Biology.

questions.q: In the frequentist view, what is the probability of an event?
options: The long-run fraction of times it occurs in repeated trials
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.2: The Bayesian view treats probability as degree of belief.
A is wrong: That is the Bayesian view.
B is wrong: Probabilities vary.
C is wrong: That is a count.

questions.q: Who set out the axioms of probability in 1933?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.3: Probabilities lie between zero and one, the whole space has probability one, and disjoint probabilities add.
B is wrong: Pascal worked with Fermat in 1654.
C is wrong: Bayes's paper appeared in 1763.
D is wrong: Gauss is linked to the normal distribution.

questions.q: What is P(A or B) for any two events?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.4: The overlap would otherwise be counted twice.
B is wrong: That holds only for disjoint events.
C is wrong: That is P(A and B) for independent events.
D is wrong: That is the complement of A.

questions.q: With two fair dice, what is the probability of a total of seven?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.5: Six of the thirty-six equally likely outcomes total seven.
A is wrong: There are six ways, not three.
C is wrong: Only six outcomes total seven.
D is wrong: That is one specific ordered outcome.

questions.q: In how many ways can five books be arranged on a shelf?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.7: n different objects can be arranged in n! ways.
A is wrong: That is 5².
B is wrong: Order matters.
D is wrong: That is 5⁵.

questions.q: How many five-card hands can be dealt from a 52-card deck?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.8: Order does not matter in a hand.
A is wrong: That counts ordered draws with replacement.
B is wrong: That counts ordered hands.
C is wrong: That is 52 × 5.

questions.q: In a room of twenty-three people, about what is the chance that at least two share a birthday?
options: Just over one half, about 50.7 per cent
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.9: The chance all differ is about 0.493.
B is wrong: That is roughly 23/365.
C is wrong: Pairs grow much faster than people.
D is wrong: Certainty needs 366 people.

questions.q: A product has one hundred components, each with a 1 per cent chance of a defect. About what is the chance of at least one defect?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.11: 1 − 0.99¹⁰⁰ ≈ 0.634.
A is wrong: Small risks add up.
C is wrong: It is not certain.
D is wrong: That is the chance of no defect.

questions.q: What is the Monte Carlo method?
options: A formula for the normal distribution
Estimating probabilities by repeating a simulated experiment many times with random numbers
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.13: Developed by Ulam, von Neumann, and colleagues.
A is wrong: It is a simulation method.
B is wrong: That is factorial counting.
C is wrong: It estimates by simulation.

questions.q: About what is the probability of drawing two aces without replacement?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.2: After the first ace, three aces remain among fifty-one cards.
A is wrong: That assumes replacement.
B is wrong: Probabilities of a sequence multiply.
D is wrong: That is one ace.

questions.q: Two machines make 60 and 40 per cent of parts with defect rates 1 and 3 per cent. What is the overall defect rate?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.4: 0.6 × 1% + 0.4 × 3% = 0.6% + 1.2% = 1.8%.
A is wrong: That is the unweighted average.
B is wrong: That adds the rates.
C is wrong: That is only the second machine's contribution.

questions.q: When are two events independent?
options: When P(A | B) = P(A), equivalently P(A and B) = P(A) P(B)
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.5: Knowing one occurred does not change the other's probability.
B is wrong: Disjoint events with positive probability are dependent.
C is wrong: Equal probabilities do not imply independence.
D is wrong: That is strong dependence.

questions.q: Why is independence an assumption to justify rather than a default in reliability?
options: Because series systems are always reliable
Components can fail together from common causes such as a power surge or fire
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.6: Common-cause failures are central in aircraft and nuclear safety.
A is wrong: They do for independent events.
B is wrong: They do.
C is wrong: Series systems compound risk.

questions.q: Ten independent components, each 99 per cent reliable, are in series. About how reliable is the system?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.7: 0.99¹⁰ ≈ 0.904; every component must work.
B is wrong: Series reliability is the product.
C is wrong: That would be a redundant system.
D is wrong: The product is far larger.

questions.q: What does Bayes' theorem state?
options: P(B | A) = P(A | B) P(B) / P(A)
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.8: The denominator usually comes from the law of total probability.
B is wrong: Conditional probabilities are not symmetric.
C is wrong: That is not Bayes' theorem.
D is wrong: That is independence.

questions.q: A disease affects 1 per cent; a test detects 99 per cent of cases and gives 2 per cent false positives. What is P(disease | positive)?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.10: Of 297 positives per 10,000, 99 are true.
A is wrong: That ignores the base rate.
B is wrong: That is the false-positive rate.
C is wrong: False positives outnumber true ones two to one.

questions.q: What is the base-rate fallacy?
options: Ignoring the prior probability of the condition when interpreting a test
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.11: When the condition is rare, false positives can outnumber true positives.
A is wrong: Sample size is not the issue.
C is wrong: That is the gambler's fallacy.
D is wrong: That is a different error.

questions.q: In the Monty Hall problem, what is the probability of winning if you switch?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.13: Your first choice was right only one third of the time.
A is wrong: The host's knowledge makes the doors unequal.
C is wrong: That is the chance if you stay.
D is wrong: Switching can still lose.

questions.q: What is the expected value of a fair die?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.2: (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6)/6 = 3.5; it need not be a possible value.
B is wrong: The average of 1 to 6 is 3.5.
C is wrong: That is the maximum.
D is wrong: That is the sum, not divided by six.

questions.q: What is the expected total of two dice?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.3: By linearity, 3.5 + 3.5 = 7, independence not required.
A is wrong: That is the maximum.
C is wrong: That is one die.
D is wrong: The mean of each die is 3.5.

questions.q: Which formula gives the variance of X?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.4: For a fair die it is 35/12, about 2.92.
A is wrong: The square of the mean alone is not the variance.
B is wrong: The order is reversed.
D is wrong: The square of the mean is subtracted.

questions.q: What are the mean and variance of a Bernoulli variable with success probability p?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.5: It equals one with probability p and zero otherwise.
A is wrong: The mean is p.
B is wrong: The variance is p(1 − p).
C is wrong: 1/p is the geometric mean.

questions.q: Parts have a 2 per cent defect rate; an inspector samples twenty. About what is the chance of no defectives?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.7: 0.98²⁰ ≈ 0.668; the expected number is 0.4.
A is wrong: That is one part.
B is wrong: 0.4 is the expected number of defectives.
D is wrong: That is the defect rate.

questions.q: If each attempt succeeds with probability 1/10, how many attempts are needed on average?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.8: The geometric distribution has mean 1/p.
A is wrong: 1/p = 10.
B is wrong: That is 1/p².
D is wrong: Most attempts fail.

questions.q: When does the Poisson distribution approximate the binomial?
options: When n is large and p small, with np = λ
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.10: Bortkiewicz's horse-kick data is a famous example.
A is wrong: Then the normal approximation is used.
B is wrong: That is Bernoulli.
D is wrong: It is the standard limit.

questions.q: A server averages three requests per second. About what is the probability of none in a given second?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.11: The Poisson probability of zero is e^(−λ).
A is wrong: That is the probability of exactly three.
B is wrong: No requests is possible.
C is wrong: That is 1/3, not e⁻³.

questions.q: Why are ice cream sales and drownings positively correlated?
options: Both rise in hot weather; correlation is not causation
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.13: Correlation also measures only linear association.
A is wrong: There is a common cause.
B is wrong: There is a common cause.
D is wrong: They are positively correlated.

questions.q: What is the variance of the uniform distribution on [a, b]?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.3: Its mean is the midpoint (a + b)/2.
A is wrong: That is half the width.
B is wrong: That is the mean.
D is wrong: The factor 1/12 is needed.

questions.q: If requests arrive at three per second, what is the mean time between them?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.4: Exponential waiting times have mean 1/λ.
A is wrong: That inverts the rate.
C is wrong: The rate is three per second.
D is wrong: That is a probability, not a mean.

questions.q: What does it mean that the exponential distribution is memoryless?
options: The chance of surviving another t hours does not depend on how long the item has lasted
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.5: It suits components in useful life, not parts that wear out.
A is wrong: They vary randomly.
B is wrong: That is wear-out, not memorylessness.
C is wrong: Its mean is 1/λ.

questions.q: About what fraction of a normal distribution lies within two standard deviations of the mean?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.7: The 68–95–99.7 rule.
A is wrong: That is within one.
B is wrong: That is within three.
C is wrong: Half lies on each side of the mean.

questions.q: How do you standardise a normal variable X?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.8: Z has mean zero and standard deviation one.
B is wrong: Subtract the mean, divide by σ.
C is wrong: The roles are swapped.
D is wrong: That is not standardisation.

questions.q: What is the standard error of the mean of n independent measurements with standard deviation σ?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.10: Variances add, so the variance of the mean is σ²/n.
B is wrong: Precision improves only with the square root.
C is wrong: Averaging reduces spread.
D is wrong: That is the spread of the sum.

questions.q: What does the law of large numbers say?
options: As n grows, the sample mean converges to the true mean
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.11: It justifies repeating measurements and averaging.
A is wrong: That is not the law.
C is wrong: That is the central limit theorem.
D is wrong: The variance of the mean decreases.

questions.q: What does the central limit theorem state?
options: The distribution of a sample mean of many independent variables with finite variance approaches a normal distribution
Sample means always equal the true mean
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.12: This holds whatever the shape of each variable's distribution.
A is wrong: Only sums and averages approach normality.
C is wrong: That is approached by the law of large numbers.
D is wrong: That is not the theorem.

questions.q: Why does the sample variance divide by n − 1?
options: Because one measurement is always discarded
To make the variance larger than any data value
To estimate the population variance without bias, since deviations are measured from the sample mean
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.2: The sample mean estimates the population mean.
A is wrong: No data are discarded.
B is wrong: That is not the purpose.
D is wrong: n is known.

questions.q: Who developed maximum likelihood estimation?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.3: The estimate maximises the probability of the observed data.
B is wrong: Gosset discovered the t distribution.
C is wrong: Bayes wrote on inverse probability.
D is wrong: Shewhart developed control charts.

questions.q: A coin lands heads k times in n tosses. What is the maximum likelihood estimate of p?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.4: Maximising p^k (1 − p)^(n − k) gives p̂ = k/n.
A is wrong: The estimate depends on the data.
C is wrong: That inverts the ratio.
D is wrong: That is the odds.

questions.q: With known σ, what is a 95 per cent confidence interval for the mean of normal data?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.5: 1.96 standard errors either side of the sample mean.
A is wrong: The standard error σ/√n is needed.
B is wrong: The multiplier and the square root are missing.
C is wrong: That is a different rule.

questions.q: A poll of one thousand finds 50 per cent support. About what is the 95 per cent margin of error?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.8: Standard error √(0.25/1000) ≈ 1.6 points; doubled gives about 3.
A is wrong: That is one standard error.
B is wrong: Far too wide for n = 1000.
D is wrong: Far too narrow.

questions.q: What can be said directly of a Bayesian 95 per cent credible interval?
options: It is identical to a confidence interval in meaning
It contains 95 per cent of the data
Given the data and the prior, there is a 95 per cent probability the parameter lies in it
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.11: A confidence interval does not allow that statement for a single interval.
A is wrong: Their interpretations differ.
B is wrong: It concerns the parameter.
D is wrong: It depends on the prior.

questions.q: What is a p-value?
options: The probability, assuming the null hypothesis, of a statistic at least as extreme as observed
The probability that the null hypothesis is true
The probability the result is important
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.2: A small p-value counts as evidence against the null.
B is wrong: That is a common misreading.
C is wrong: Significance is not importance.
D is wrong: That is chosen in advance.

questions.q: A coin tossed 400 times gives 225 heads. What is the standardised value under fairness?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.3: Mean 200 and standard deviation 10, so (225 − 200)/10 = 2.5.
B is wrong: One must divide by the standard deviation.
C is wrong: The standard deviation is 10, not 100.
D is wrong: The standard deviation is √(400 × 0.25) = 10.

questions.q: What is a type I error?
options: Failing to reject a false null
Rejecting a true null hypothesis: a false alarm
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.4: Its probability is the significance level.
A is wrong: That is type II.
C is wrong: That is power.
D is wrong: That affects power, not the definition.

questions.q: If twenty independent tests are run at the 5 per cent level with no real effects, about what is the chance of at least one false alarm?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.7: 1 − 0.95²⁰ ≈ 0.64.
A is wrong: That is per test.
B is wrong: It is not certain.
C is wrong: Probabilities do not simply multiply by twenty here.

questions.q: What is the slope of the least-squares regression line?
options: The covariance of x and y divided by the variance of x
The variance of y divided by the variance of x
The mean of y divided by the mean of x
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.9: The line passes through the point of means.
A is wrong: Correlation is unitless.
C is wrong: The covariance is needed.
D is wrong: That ignores co-variation.

questions.q: What are principles of Fisher's design of experiments?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.11: They make data collection efficient and conclusions valid.
A is wrong: These are pitfalls.
B is wrong: Replication is a principle.
D is wrong: That invites bias.

questions.q: Where are the limits on a Shewhart control chart usually set?
options: About three standard deviations from the process mean
At the product specification limits only
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.12: Points outside suggest the process has changed.
B is wrong: That would flag half of all points.
C is wrong: Far too tight.
D is wrong: Control limits reflect process variation.
